## The Museum of Unfinished Things

At the end of the harbor, where the fishing boats grew tired and the gulls stopped bothering even the most succulent scraps, there was a museum that appeared only on rainy Tuesdays.

Its doors were painted green, though no one could agree on what color green meant there. The windows displayed ordinary objects: a letter without an address, a violin missing three strings, a wooden house with no windows, a map of a country that had never existed.

Above the entrance, a brass sign read:

**MUSEUM OF UNFINISHED THINGS**  
*Open whenever you are ready to be disappointed.*

Admission was free, but visitors were asked to bring one thing they had started and would never complete.

At the door, the curator—a small, solemn man with a beard that seemed to contain several unfinished beards—examined what I carried.

“A sandcastle,” he said.

“Does that count?”

“It has potential.”

He stamped my ticket with a tiny silver tower and stepped aside.

Inside, the museum was much larger than the building outside. Rooms stretched farther than perspective allowed. In the first gallery stood paintings of landscapes interrupted by blank spaces. One showed a storm approaching a field, but the field ended in an unmarked white edge. Another depicted a woman reaching toward a doorway, though the doorway had been left out entirely.

“No artist ever finished this one,” the curator explained. “They became distracted by a beautiful thought.”

“What happened to it?”

“We keep the thought. It’s in the basement.”

Downstairs was the archive of unwritten endings. I saw manuscripts with final pages torn away, diaries whose last entries were missing, and a stack of recipes labeled only **Soup, Eventually**.

In one glass case lay a watch that ticked backward toward an hour no one remembered.

In another rested a red mitten.

“No match,” said the curator. “But perhaps someday.”

I wandered into a room filled with half-built bridges. They hovered over miniature valleys, their far ends suspended in the air. Workers’ tools lay beside them, abandoned with dust on their handles.

“Why leave them?” I asked.

“Because completion can be cruel,” he said. “Once a bridge is finished, it becomes merely a bridge. Before that, it is a promise.”

I thought of all the things I had abandoned: songs learned halfway, novels with sleepy endings, conversations continued only in my head, plans made with enthusiasm and dissolved like sugar in rain. Looking at the unfinished bridges, I did not feel accused. I felt accompanied.

Near the back of the museum was a narrow staircase spiraling upward. At its top was a door marked **THE EXHIBITION YOU DID NOT EXPECT**.

The curator checked his watch.

“That room is closed,” he said.

“Why?”

“Because nobody has ever entered it.”

“Then how do we know it exists?”

He smiled. “Good question. Please do not answer it.”

I pushed open the door.

The room beyond was bright, though it had no visible windows. Paintings covered the walls, every one of them complete. There were finished bridges spanning bright chasms, entire novels bound in gold, songs performed by full orchestras, sunsets that reached the horizon without a single blank edge.

In the center of the room stood a small wooden house. It had windows, a chimney, a crooked but sturdy roof, and a light burning in the kitchen.

A note was nailed to the front door:

**This house was built by someone who later became distracted by a beautiful thought. Please admire it briefly, but do not stay forever. There are unfinished things outside, and they need you.**

Behind me, the curator’s voice floated up the stairs.

“We close at five,” he called. “But not today.”

I entered the house.

Inside, a table had been set for two. Steam rose from a kettle. A cat slept beneath a chair, though its other half was nowhere to be seen. Through the window, I could see the museum grounds, and beyond them the gray harbor and the restless sea.

On the table lay two cups, a bowl of lemons, and a sheet of paper covered in handwriting.

The first line read:

*Today I began a story about a museum that appeared only on rainy Tuesdays.*

I read the sentence, and a drop of rain struck the window.

Then another.

The story on the page continued, one line at a time, in handwriting that looked exactly like mine.
